title: LLM Knowledge Bases: a practical guide — Ben Holmes, Warp

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 51%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is designing an LLM knowledge base from disorganized notes. The pipeline builds a personal knowledge base for individual productivity. The presentation covers designing the pipeline, prototyping the enrich skill, and deploying automated cloud runs. It requires familiarity with CLI tools and prompt engineering but remains a practical guide for builders. The speaker demonstrates voice dictation, the enrich skill, and wiki generation throughout the talk. All provided evidence anchors are explicitly said in the transcript.

summary: Ben Holmes introduces the problem of disorganized notes that most people accumulate in Apple Notes or similar apps. His goal is to transform a raw folder of markdown notes into an organized, navigable, and interconnected knowledge base. The pipeline begins with capturing raw thoughts via voice dictation, which at roughly 200 words per minute is faster than typing. He recommends local, on-device tools like Handy (open source) and Voice Ink ($20 lifetime fee) to avoid subscription costs. The capture step is deliberately sloppy because volume of raw material matters more than polish. The next stage is an enrich note agent skill that stamps each file with an enrichment timestamp so later runs skip already-processed notes, assigns tags from a fixed reference list to prevent the model from inventing new categories, researches the source on the web, and finds backlinks to related notes via key term search. He notes that Claude tends to get creative with tags and must be instructed to be reluctant about adding new ones. Beyond enrichment, wikis can be generated on top of the notes, grouping people, concepts, organizations, and sources. This idea comes from an Andrej Karpathy gist: take a raw directory and combine it into a focus area you care about, producing organized browsable entries. He shows wikis for AI news, music/AI intersections, and Bible study characters. For work contexts, wikis can generate people sections with backlinks to related meetings and source links. The whole pipeline runs on automated schedules in a cloud sandbox via oz.dev (warp.dev/os). The Obsidian headless CLI syncs markdown down into the sandbox, the agent enriches unprocessed notes or regenerates the wiki, then syncs back—so you wake up to a fresh wiki like a personal daily paper. Local automations like Codex app require your laptop to be open, so cloud scheduling is preferred. Finally, he shows a graph view of every note built purely by asking an agent to create HTML and Tailwind visualizations. The graph reveals clusters of interests and gaps in thinking, with clickable nodes. He also shows a habit-tracker burndown chart generated the same way. His open-source notes app hub.md provides an agent-accessible Apple Notes alternative.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the disorganized notes problem
sections.summary: Ben Holmes introduces himself as Warp's developer relations lead and asks the audience about their disorganized Apple Notes folders and Obsidian usage. He frames the talk around organizing raw thoughts and notes into something navigable and discoverable.

sections.title: Pipeline overview: raw notes to browsable wiki
sections.summary: Outlines the pipeline: start with a raw folder of markdown notes, enrich notes with backlinks and tags, generate wikis over people/concepts/sources, and create visualizations like graph views using HTML via agents.

sections.title: Getting raw thoughts down via voice dictation
sections.summary: Argues voice dictation at ~200 wpm is the fastest capture method. Recommends local on-device tools: Handy (open source) and Voice Ink ($20 lifetime). Emphasizes being scrappy and prioritizing volume over formatting.

sections.title: Enriching notes with an agent skill
sections.summary: Shows an enriched note with tags, source URL, enrichment timestamp, and backlinks. Details the enrich note skill: stamp timestamps, generate tags from a fixed reference folder, instruct the agent to be reluctant about new tags, research sources via web tools, and find backlinks via key term search.

sections.title: Running the enrich skill and automation
sections.summary: Demonstrates running the enrich note skill in Warp. Shows a completed automated run that processes all notes lacking enrichment timestamps, creating a more organized notebook.

sections.title: Browsing enriched notes and generating wikis
sections.summary: Shows enriched notes from The Left Hand of Darkness with click-through related note navigation. Introduces wiki generation over notes grouping people, concepts, and sources. Shows an AI news wiki and a music/AI intersection wiki.

sections.title: Karpathy gist and wiki generation for varied topics
sections.summary: Explains that wiki generation is based on an Andrej Karpathy gist: take a raw directory and combine it into a focus area. Shows a Bible in a Year podcast wiki with character entries and references. Discusses workplace applications: meeting notes wikis with people sections, backlinks to related meetings, and source links back to raw notes.

sections.title: Automating the pipeline on a schedule
sections.summary: Covers running enrichment and wiki generation on automated schedules. Contrasts local automations (Codex app, requires laptop open) with cloud scheduling via oz.dev. Describes the flow: Obsidian headless CLI syncs markdown into a cloud sandbox, the agent enriches unprocessed notes or updates the wiki, then syncs back. Shows the oz.dev prompt instructing the agent to pull down, update, and sync back up.

sections.title: Waking up to a fresh wiki and reviewing cloud runs
sections.summary: Describes waking up to a perfectly fresh wiki like a personal daily paper. Shows a cloud run viewable in the browser where notes taken throughout the day were enriched overnight. Reviews the Ferrari note now with podcast source link, heading, and related notes.

sections.title: Visualizing notes with graph views and charts
sections.summary: Shows a graph view of all notes built by asking an agent to use HTML and Tailwind. Clusters reveal interests (books, startup founding, AI/engineering, faith/scripture) and gaps in thinking. Nodes are clickable and the layout can be changed to a space constellation. Also shows a habit-tracker burndown chart generated the same way.

sections.title: Closing tools and self-promotion
sections.summary: Plugs oz.dev (warp.dev/os) for scheduling automations and hub.md, a free open-source agent-accessible notes app open to contributions. Promotes himself as developer relations at Warp, mentions the booth, Twitter, and a side event tonight.

demonstrations: Demonstrates Voice Ink hotkey dictation producing formatted paragraphs from spoken input after listening to the Acquired podcast about Walt Disney.

limitations: Voice dictation can be awkward in office environments with coworkers around.
Claude tends to invent new tags unless explicitly instructed to use a fixed reference list.
The pipeline requires a large volume of raw notes to be effective for wiki generation and visualization.
Local automations like Codex app require your laptop to be open when the task runs.
Generating wikis with agents can take time, necessitating background scheduling.
quantitativeClaims: Voice dictation averages about 200 words per minute.
Voice Ink costs a $20 lifetime fee for app updates.
